Funguys Swarm, developed and published by Stairway Games, is a chaotic, fast-paced roguelite bullet hell that blends humor, action, and charm into a surprisingly addictive survival experience. Set in a whimsical forest overrun by fire-based enemies, the game tasks you with playing as a brave little mushroom—or “Funguy”—who must battle increasingly overwhelming waves of enemies while collecting upgrades, saving forest creatures, and gradually building a community. Beneath its cartoonish visuals and absurd premise lies a cleverly designed game that rewards creativity, experimentation, and reflexes in equal measure. The gameplay loop is simple in structure but rich in execution. Each run begins with your chosen Funguy character armed with a weapon—anything from a Watermelon Axe to a Garlic Hammer—and thrown into a hostile arena. Waves of enemies, from possessed carrots to flame-throwing vegetation, swarm the screen as you dodge, attack, and collect power-ups. After each round, you're offered a choice of upgrades that radically affect your build, allowing for wild combinations of skills and weapons. It's in these moments that Funguys Swarm shines brightest. The freedom to mix and match upgrades results in unpredictable yet satisfying builds, encouraging players to experiment and improvise. No two runs feel the same, and the escalating chaos is where the game finds its rhythm. What makes the experience even more compelling is the persistent progression system. As you rescue friendly forest creatures during runs, they return to your home base—known as the Sanctuary—where they unlock permanent upgrades and features. This loop between short-term roguelite chaos and long-term progression offers a sense of accomplishment even after failed attempts. It’s a rewarding system that balances challenge with accessibility, making each run feel like it’s contributing to something larger. The Sanctuary also gives the game a cozy narrative backbone, reminding players that there's a community worth fighting for amid the madness. Visually, the game embraces a playful, vibrant art style that sets it apart from the often gritty or dark aesthetics of the genre. Characters are expressive, animations are bouncy, and each biome—from the Carrot Farm to the Frozen Pond—is rendered with charming detail. The contrast between the whimsical art and the intensity of bullet hell combat adds to the game’s unique identity. Sound design also contributes to the game’s energetic tone, with upbeat music and satisfying effects that enhance the action without overwhelming the senses. The user interface is colorful and functional, though it can feel slightly cluttered during heavy combat sequences—a common growing pain in early access titles. Being an early access game, Funguys Swarm is still evolving. As of its launch, it features two characters, three core weapons, a growing list of skills, and a couple of biomes to explore. While content is currently limited compared to more mature roguelites, the foundation is strong, and the developer has already begun rolling out patches and responding to player feedback. A recent hotfix addressed issues with skill rerolling, UI responsiveness, and performance—demonstrating a clear commitment to iterative improvement. There are occasional hiccups, such as minor bugs or rare crashes, but nothing game-breaking or out of the ordinary for early access. The gameplay itself is stable, and the developers are transparent about their roadmap. Community involvement is another highlight. The developers actively engage with players via feedback forums and update blogs, and future plans include more weapons, new enemies, additional biomes, and expanded story elements. There's also a fun bit of crossover for fans of Coral Island, another Stairway Games project, with unlockable cosmetic items that connect the two universes. This shared-world approach is a subtle but effective way to build brand identity and community loyalty. While it may not yet have the sheer volume of content found in giants of the genre like Vampire Survivors or Hades, Funguys Swarm is clearly on the path to becoming something special. It combines the frenetic joy of bullet hell shooters with the satisfying depth of roguelite progression, all wrapped in a charming, forest-fantasy aesthetic that feels refreshing in a genre that can often take itself too seriously. For players who enjoy quick sessions, chaotic build variety, and quirky humor with surprising depth, Funguys Swarm is an easy recommendation—especially for those who appreciate being part of a game’s journey from its early roots to full bloom. Rating: 9/10

Funguys Swarm is visually fantastic and feels great to play. For an Early Access title, the level of content and overall polish is impressive. It is clearly worth the price, but there are several things holding it back from being recommended from me currently. [b]Main issues I had - [/b] [i]Missing Settings:[/i] There are currently no options to adjust graphics or rebind keys. [i]Performance:[/i] While it runs fine on PC, the Steam Deck performance chokes significantly during swarms. [i]On-Death Effects:[/i] This is my biggest gripe. Enemies are often more dangerous dead than alive, and the reaction windows are too tight. Almost all my deaths felt cheap rather than earned. [i] Visual Clarity: [/i] Projectiles can easily get lost in the chaos of a swarm. Similarly, buildings sometimes obstruct your view; I’ve taken damage from enemies hidden behind bridges or buildings enough times to be frustrated. [i] Environmental Hazards:[/i] Level 2’s ice is more frustrating than challenging. Losing character control is rarely "fun," and sliding into enemies feels cheap. Level 3’s lava is better, but it needs a clearer UI indicator (on-screen rather than just on the character) to track damage ticks. [i] Mobility vs. Hazards:[/i] The game seems to expect more dashes than it gives you. If you’re caught in a telegraphed red circle without a dash charge, you’re often hit regardless of your movement speed. Either give more dashes, more native movespeed, or make it so on death effects take much longer to explode. This game has a very bright future, but it needs a bit more time in the oven. I’m giving it a Not Recommended for now simply because Steam lacks a neutral option, but with a few patches, this could easily be a must-play. It's very polished but also equally frustrating.

用這個價格玩到這樣的美術和動畫設計真的很棒，不過感覺數值設計真的很糟糕，感覺只是無腦拉高怪的血量，大部分Rogue遊戲入場玩到一半的程度，至少攻擊力還可以勉強應付周圍的小怪進攻，但大部分沒辦法，除非一路上可以選到對的技能，不然大部分是沒辦法過的，只能靠一直死來升級永久技能來堆高等級而推動進度，角色和敵人大小顏色非常相似，本應可以用降低敵人子彈和本身飽和度來改善畫面分不清楚的問題，可是感覺一直不想改善 ------------------------------------------------------------- The art and animation design are truly impressive for this price point. However, the numerical balancing feels terrible. It seems like they just brainlessly inflated the enemies' health pools. In most Roguelike games, by the mid-point of a run, your attack power should at least be enough to handle basic mobs, but that’s rarely the case here. Unless you get lucky with the perfect skill synergy, it’s nearly impossible to progress. You're forced to rely on 'death grinding'—dying repeatedly to upgrade permanent stats just to push forward. Furthermore, the character and enemy sprites are way too similar in size and color. This visual clutter could have been fixed by lowering the saturation of enemy bullets or the environment, but it feels like the developers have no intention of improving this.
